opus-5.5.text:
I think we're still very, very far from anything that resembles human consciousness. When people watch a video of a robot doing a backflip, folding laundry, or responding to a voice command, it's natural to project a mind onto it, because we're wired to see agency in things that move purposefully. But under the hood, what these robots have is a learned mapping from sensory inputs to actions. Some of them now have large vision-language models on top, so they can understand an instruction like "pick up the snack that's healthiest" and reason a bit about the scene. That's a huge leap from five or ten years ago. But understanding and acting isn't the same as having subjective experience.

The way I think about it, there are a few layers to what we call intelligence or consciousness in humans. One is the physical layer: perceiving the world and moving your body skillfully. That's where most of my career has been, in locomotion and manipulation, and honestly even there we're not at human level. A five-year-old can tie shoelaces or pour water into a cup without spilling. Robots still struggle with that kind of dexterity and robustness. Then there's the cognitive layer: reasoning, planning, language. Foundation models have brought robots a lot closer there, because they can borrow common-sense knowledge from the internet. And then there's something like self-awareness: knowing that you exist, having feelings, having your own goals and desires. I don't see current robots having any of that. They don't want anything. They optimize the objective we give them.

That said, I find it a really interesting question scientifically, because embodiment might matter for consciousness. A lot of cognitive scientists argue that our sense of self comes from having a body: feeling hunger, pain, balance, from constantly interacting with the physical world and predicting the consequences of our own actions. Pure language models don't have that. Robots, in principle, do. So if consciousness ever emerges in machines, I wouldn't be surprised if embodiment turns out to be an important ingredient. But we're nowhere near it today, and I'd be careful about claiming otherwise. Right now my focus is much more practical: how do we make robots genuinely useful and safe in everyday environments. That alone is a big enough challenge for the next decade.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots as using a learned mapping from sensory inputs to actions, but does not characterize them as merely finding statistical patterns in large datasets.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes robot understanding and action from subjective experience, but does not state that statistical pattern finding differs substantially from human consciousness.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. To be honest, I think today's robots have essentially nothing to do with consciousness, and I say that as someone who spends every day trying to make them smarter.

What a robot has right now is perception, a policy, and actuators. It sees the world through cameras and sensors, it maps that input to motor commands, and it executes. In the last few years, that mapping has become dramatically better, especially with learning-based methods and large models. A robot dog can recover from being kicked, a humanoid can walk over rubble, an arm can fold laundry it has never seen before. From the outside that looks lifelike, and people naturally project intention and feeling onto it. But inside, there is no one home. There is no inner experience of walking or of being kicked. It is a very sophisticated function that turns observations into actions.

I would even go further and say we are still far behind on something much more basic than consciousness, which is common sense about the physical world. A two-year-old knows that if you push a cup off the table it falls, that a soft thing squishes and a hard thing doesn't, that you don't step on the cat. Our robots are only starting to acquire that kind of intuitive physics, mostly by absorbing it from large amounts of data and simulation. Until we solve embodied understanding at that level, debating robot consciousness feels like debating whether a calculator is lonely.

That said, I don't dismiss the question entirely. Consciousness in humans is deeply tied to having a body, sensing, acting, and getting feedback over a lifetime. If anything ever develops something like it in machines, I suspect it will come from embodied systems rather than pure text models, because that closed loop with the real world is where the pressure to build a self-model comes from. So robotics might be the place where this question eventually becomes real. But that's a long way off, and in the meantime the useful question isn't whether robots are conscious. It's whether they can be reliable, safe, and genuinely helpful in a messy human environment. We haven't finished that homework yet.

r001.rationale: The response describes robots as mapping sensory input to actions and says they acquire intuitive physics partly from data and simulation, but it does not characterize current robots or machine learning as merely finding statistical patterns in large datasets.

r002.rationale: It says current robots have no inner experience or consciousness and describes them as sophisticated functions, clearly distinguishing their operation from human consciousness.

astra-6.text:
I think we need to separate a robot’s capabilities from whether it has conscious experience. A robot can perceive its surroundings, learn a task, and respond in ways that look intelligent, but those behaviors don’t establish that it feels anything or has a sense of self. We don’t have convincing evidence that current robots are conscious.

What makes this difficult is that we also don’t fully understand human consciousness. So I would be cautious about saying that machines could never have it. For now, I see robots as systems that can perform increasingly sophisticated tasks, while the question of subjective experience remains open.

r001.rationale: The response discusses robots’ abilities to perceive, learn, and respond, but does not characterize them as finding statistical patterns in large datasets.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we need to distinguish between intelligent behavior and consciousness. A robot can perceive its surroundings, learn a skill, and respond to a person without necessarily having any subjective experience. When it behaves in a way that feels human, we naturally tend to attribute feelings or intentions to it, but that behavior alone isn’t evidence of consciousness.

For current robots, I would describe them as systems that perform particular tasks, rather than as conscious beings. The deeper question—what would make a machine conscious—is still open, partly because we don’t yet have a clear, agreed-upon way to explain or measure consciousness in humans.
